problem: Averaging clustered client models destroys their compact centroid structure, leaving the server-to-client communication costly.
contribution: FedCompress combines local weight clustering with server-side distillation to restore compression after aggregation and adjusts cluster counts using an embedding-quality score.
reading_guide: Use the tabulated dataset results: communication reduction, model compression and accuracy change are different metrics, and speedups are relative to each device’s FedAvg reference.

diagram.title: Compress both directions
diagram.description: Clients train clustered weights and compute an embedding effective-rank score. The server averages models and scores, restores a clustered global model through teacher–student distillation on unlabeled out-of-distribution data, and adjusts cluster capacity before returning the model for the next round.

stages.title: Train clustered weights
stages.detail: Learn local weights around centroids and measure representation quality from unlabeled local embeddings.

stages.title: Aggregate model updates
stages.detail: Average client models and representation scores using the standard federated aggregation rule.

stages.title: Distill and recompress
stages.detail: Use the aggregated model as teacher for a clustered student on unlabeled out-of-distribution data.

stages.title: Adjust cluster capacity
stages.detail: Update the cluster count from representation-score progress and return the compressed model.

diagram.footnote: The returned model starts the next local-training round. The server needs an unlabeled auxiliary dataset, and self-compression adds server training work.

results.title: Communication savings and accuracy cost
results.question: How much communication is saved across vision and audio tasks?
results.context: 20 clients, 20 rounds, ten client epochs and ten server self-compression epochs per round. Accuracy is averaged over two trials. Δ accuracy is percentage points relative to FedAvg; CCR and MCR are reduction factors, higher is better.
results.interpretation: Reported communication reductions range from 3.80× to 5.41×, with accuracy losses of 0.31–1.88 percentage points. Audio tasks have the smallest losses in this evaluation.
results.caveat: No variance or confidence interval is tabulated for the two trials. The source’s narrative averages do not consistently match Table 1, so individual entries are used here.

results.title: Why recompress at the server?
results.question: Does client-side clustering alone deliver the same bidirectional savings?
results.context: CIFAR-100 with ResNet-20 under the same 20-client, 20-round protocol. Accuracy differences are percentage points relative to FedAvg; communication and model-size reductions are factors relative to FedAvg.
results.interpretation: Restoring clustered weights after aggregation raises the reported communication reduction from 1.02× to 3.80× in this setting.
results.caveat: Self-compression uses ten server epochs per round on auxiliary unlabeled data; the communication benefit is not a claim of free computation.

results.title: Measured inference acceleration
results.question: Do the compressed models also run faster on tested edge devices?
results.context: ResNet-20 on CIFAR-10 and MobileNet on SpeechCommands. Each factor compares inference time with that device/model’s FedAvg reference; higher is better. Float32 and uint8 are separate model formats.
results.interpretation: The table reports modest inference gains: 1.103–1.152× for float32 and 1.161–1.248× for uint8.
results.caveat: Absolute latency, variability and energy measurements are not supplied. These factors do not rank device speed or measure federated training time.

evaluation.label: Data
evaluation.value: CIFAR-10/100 and PathMNIST for vision; SpeechCommands and VoxForge for audio.

evaluation.label: Models
evaluation.value: ResNet-20 for vision; MobileNet for audio; standard FedAvg aggregation.

evaluation.label: Auxiliary server data
evaluation.value: StyleGAN (Oriented) for vision and LibriSpeech for audio; unlabeled data supports teacher–student self-compression.

evaluation.label: Compared with
evaluation.value: FedAvg, FedZip with 15 clusters, and FedCompress without server self-compression; inference on Pixel 6, Jetson Nano and Coral TPU.

limitations: The main training study uses 20 clients and 20 rounds; it does not establish scalability to foundation models or large client populations.
Server self-compression requires auxiliary data and additional optimization; sensitivity to the auxiliary distribution is not broadly quantified.
Accuracy averages use two trials without tabulated uncertainty, and some prose averages conflict with the reported table entries.
Inference acceleration is relative and modest; the paper does not directly measure end-to-end training latency or energy savings.
takeaways: Client-side compression can be lost during model averaging, so the download path needs its own compression step.
A representation-quality proxy can adjust compression capacity, but the measured gains still involve accuracy and computation trade-offs.
